title: Rerum Novarum (1891)
hook: Leo XIII writes on workers: fair wages, unions and dignity

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Bosco and the boys of Turin. Your line was reason, faith, kindness. Which young person did you encourage? Today, a pope writes about the factory floor. Day eight hundred ninety-five.

A factory whistle before sunrise. Men, women and children walk in through the gate, and they will not walk out until dark. The pay barely covers bread and rent. If someone is hurt at the machine, there is often no help and no job tomorrow. In the cities of the new industrial age, people argued hard about what to do. Some said the owners owed nothing beyond the agreed wage. Others said the whole system should be torn down. And then a pope, Leo the Thirteenth, sent a letter to the bishops of the world, and it was about workers.
screen: `A FACTORY WHISTLE BEFORE DAWN.` → `TWO LOUD ANSWERS.` → `A POPE WRITES ABOUT WORKERS.`

segments.voice: Papal letters like this are called encyclicals, and they are named for their first words in Latin. This one begins Rerum novarum, of new things. In Latin the phrase also meant upheaval, even revolution, and the letter opens on that restless spirit of change: new industries, great wealth for a few, a new kind of poverty for many. Leo makes four arguments. First, the worker is a person. Leo writes that employers must not treat workers as slaves or as tools, and must respect their dignity as human beings. Second, a just wage. An agreement about pay is not automatically fair just because both sides signed it. Leo argues that a wage must be enough for a worker who lives simply and works honestly to support himself. If hunger forces a man to accept less, that is injustice, even if it is a contract. Jesus says it plainly in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "for the labourer is worthy of his hire." Third, unions. Leo defends the right of workers to form associations, to band together for their own good. Fourth, no class war. Leo also defends private property, and he rejects the idea that owners and workers are natural enemies. Each has duties to the other, he says, and the state has a duty to protect those who are weakest. That gives us today's word, social teaching. Catholic social teaching is the body of the Church's teaching about how a society should be ordered: work, wages, property, the poor, the common good. Later popes kept returning to Rerum Novarum and building on it. Leo's answer, in the end, was that the person at the machine matters more than the machine.
screen: `RERUM NOVARUM: OF NEW THINGS.` · `NOT A TOOL. A PERSON.` · `A WAGE YOU CAN LIVE ON.` · `UNIONS, AND NO CLASS WAR.` · then, large: `WORTHY OF HIS HIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a worker by name. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day. Whose work touched your life? The person who stocked the shelves, drove the bus, cleaned the office, cooked the food, answered the phone. Pick one. Do you know their name? If you do, say it quietly to yourself. If you don't, notice that. If you pray, you can pray for them and their family. If you don't, simply hold them with respect. When the bell rings, think where you will see them next. The bell holds the time.
Social teaching. The Catholic Church's teaching on how society should be ordered, on work, wages, property and the common good. Rerum Novarum is a key letter in it.
Your line: the dignity of work. Today, learn the name of one worker who serves you, and thank them by name. Day eight hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes, schools and charities draw on the Church's social teaching in their work for fair wages, housing and the poor, and on May 1 the Church keeps the memorial of Saint Joseph the Worker.

fork.setup: it is the factory age. one side says owners owe nothing beyond the wage. the other says tear the whole system down. what does Leo XIII write?
options: side with the owners: a contract is a contract.
side with the revolution: abolish private property.

fork.reveal: Rerum Novarum defends both private property and workers' dignity, a just wage and the right to form associations.
